title: Design and Analysis of Machine Learning Experiments

sections.title: Introduction
rules: Machine learning is an empirical science that requires rigorous experimental evaluation.
We run statistical experiments to measure and validate algorithm performance.
We need formal statistical tests to confirm that observed improvements are not random chance.

sections.title: Factors, Response, and Strategy of Experimentation
rules: Factors are independent variables controlled or set by the experimenter.
Examples of factors include learning algorithms, hyperparameter values, and dataset characteristics.
Response variables are dependent outcome metrics such as classification error, runtime, and memory.
Changing one factor at a time is inefficient and cannot detect interactions between factors.
Factorial design tests all combinations of factor levels to evaluate main effects and interaction effects.

sections.title: Response Surface Design
rules: Response surface methodology explores relationships between continuous factors and response metrics.
We fit low-order polynomial models to experimental measurements across the factor space.
The fitted response surface helps find optimal hyperparameter values that minimize error.

sections.title: Randomization, Replication, and Blocking
rules: Experimental design relies on three fundamental principles: randomization, replication, and blocking.
Randomization assigns data samples and run orders randomly to eliminate systematic experimental bias.
Replication repeats experimental runs to estimate random experimental error variance accurately.
Blocking groups homogeneous experimental units together to isolate known nuisance sources of variation.
Using identical cross-validation folds across tested algorithms is a standard blocking technique.

sections.title: Guidelines for Machine Learning Experiments
rules: We must define clear experimental objectives and select meaningful response metrics.
We identify all relevant control factors, noise factors, and factor level ranges.
We select an appropriate experimental design before collecting evaluation data.
We analyze experimental results using statistical inference methods before drawing definitive conclusions.

sections.title: Cross-Validation and Resampling Methods
rules: K-fold cross-validation divides the dataset into K disjoint folds of equal size.
The model trains on K minus one folds and tests on the remaining fold.
The process repeats K times so each fold serves as the test set once.
The overall performance estimate is the average of the K test results.
In 5x2 cross-validation, we run 2-fold cross-validation five independent times.
Bootstrapping samples N instances with replacement from a dataset of size N.
On average, a bootstrap training sample contains approximately 63.2 percent of the original instances.
Unselected instances form the out-of-bag test set in the 0.632 bootstrap estimator.

sections.title: Measuring Classifier Performance
rules: A confusion matrix records counts of true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives.
Accuracy is the proportion of total test instances correctly classified.
Error rate is one minus accuracy.
Precision measures the proportion of predicted positive instances that are truly positive.
Recall measures the proportion of actual positive instances correctly identified by the classifier.
The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall.
A Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve plots true positive rate against false positive rate.
The Area Under the Curve (AUC) summarizes overall classification performance across all possible decision thresholds.

sections.title: Interval Estimation
rules: Point estimates provide a single number for an unknown population parameter.
Confidence intervals provide a range that contains the true parameter with specified probability.
The confidence level is typically set to 95 percent or 99 percent.
When sample sizes are large, the central limit theorem justifies normal distribution intervals.
For small sample sizes with unknown variance, we calculate intervals using Student's t distribution.

sections.title: Hypothesis Testing
rules: Hypothesis testing decides whether experimental evidence supports rejecting a null hypothesis.
The null hypothesis H_0 assumes no difference exists between compared learning algorithms.
The alternative hypothesis H_1 claims a statistically significant difference exists.
A Type I error occurs when we reject a true null hypothesis.
The significance level alpha is the maximum allowable probability of committing a Type I error.
A Type II error occurs when we fail to reject a false null hypothesis.
The p-value is the probability of obtaining test results as extreme as observed under H_0.
We reject the null hypothesis when the p-value is less than alpha.

sections.title: Assessing a Classification Algorithm’s Performance
rules: We test whether a classifier's error rate differs significantly from a baseline target value.
The binomial test computes exact probabilities of observed error counts on an independent test set.
When the sample size is large, we use an approximate normal z-test.
For cross-validated error rates across multiple folds, we perform a one-sample t-test.

sections.title: Comparing Two Classification Algorithms
rules: Paired tests evaluate both algorithms on the exact same test instances or data folds.
McNemar's test evaluates binary classification differences using a single shared test set.
McNemar's test examines instances where one algorithm succeeds and the other algorithm fails.
The standard paired t-test over K folds underestimates variance because training sets overlap.
Dietterich's 5x2 cross-validated paired t-test corrects for variance overlap.
Alpaydin's 5x2 cross-validated paired F-test combines all ten fold differences into an F-statistic.
The 5x2 paired F-test provides higher statistical power and lower Type I error.

sections.title: Comparing Multiple Algorithms: Analysis of Variance
rules: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) tests whether multiple algorithms have identical mean performance.
One-way ANOVA decomposes total variation into between-algorithm variation and within-algorithm error.
An F-test determines whether differences between algorithm means exceed random experimental variation.
When ANOVA rejects the null hypothesis, we run post-hoc tests to identify specific differing pairs.
Tukey's honestly significant difference test controls the family-wise error rate across all pairwise comparisons.

sections.title: Comparison over Multiple Datasets
rules: Comparing algorithms across diverse benchmark datasets requires non-parametric statistical tests.
Non-parametric tests do not assume normal distribution of algorithm performance scores.
The sign test counts how many datasets favor one algorithm over another.
The Wilcoxon signed-rank test ranks absolute performance differences between two algorithms across datasets.
The Friedman test ranks multiple algorithms on each benchmark dataset.
The Nemenyi post-hoc test calculates critical difference thresholds for pairwise algorithm comparisons.
Critical difference diagrams visualize which algorithms perform significantly better than others.

sections.title: Notes
rules: Public benchmark repositories like the UCI Machine Learning Repository promote reproducible research.
Statistical significance does not always guarantee practical significance in real-world deployment.
Testing multiple hypotheses simultaneously without correction severely inflates overall false positive rates.
Researchers must report effect sizes and confidence intervals alongside p-values.
